prompt: What question did Rafa's "usual noise" leave for this lesson?

choices.text: Why Rafa did not read the alert
choices.why: He read it; the lesson does not blame him.
Authorship is not the question.

choices.text: Why the team taught him to ignore it
choices.why: Right. Each false page taught it a little more.

choices.text: Whether the provider was really slow
choices.why: It was; that was the condition for the retry.

prompt: Which of these are symptoms of alert fatigue that the lesson names? Choose every one that applies.

choices.why: To stop the noise, meaning to look later.

choices.text: Muting an alert and forgetting it
choices.why: An hour, a day, forgotten.
Including the rare one that matters.
That can cause fatigue; it is not a symptom of it.

prompt: A team has twenty alerts, sixteen of them noisy. What does the lesson say it really has?

choices.why: Right. The noise spends the signal's credibility.

choices.text: Four good alerts and sixteen annoying ones
choices.why: That is the view the lesson argues against.

choices.text: Too few alerts to be safe
choices.why: The problem is the opposite.

choices.text: A team that needs more people on the rota
choices.why: More people would carry the same noise.

prompt: In hospitals, the same problem is called alarm ___.
Match each signal to where the lesson sends it.

pairs.left: a TLS certificate expiring in 30 days

prompt: Why does the lesson prefer alerts on symptoms over alerts on causes?

choices.why: CPU and queues are easy to measure.
They fire less often, and only when it matters.

choices.text: Causes cannot be shown on a dashboard
choices.why: The dashboard is where causes belong.

choices.text: They fire only when users are hurt
choices.why: Right. Causes fire when nothing is wrong and miss the unforeseen.

prompt: What does trying to write a runbook test about an alert?

choices.text: Whether the alert's threshold is right
choices.why: The runbook tests something else.

choices.text: Whether there is anything to do
choices.why: Right. "Look around and see" fails the question about action.

choices.text: Whether the person on call can type fast
choices.why: Speed of typing is not the point.
Any tool does.

prompt: Why do teams without a ticket queue end up with too many pages?

choices.why: Cost is not the reason given.

choices.text: Because pages are easier to write
choices.why: Both are equally easy.

choices.text: Paging becomes the only way to be seen
choices.why: Right. Every alert drifts up into the pager.

choices.text: Because tickets are read only by managers
choices.why: A ticket is read in working hours by the team.

prompt: 82 pages, 16 needed a person. What is the actionable rate, to the nearest whole percent?
How does the lesson describe the alert "card provider p99 over 2 s"?

choices.text: A cause dressed as a symptom
choices.why: Right. It fires when the provider is slow, noticed or not.
Three of its pages mattered.

choices.text: The best alert the team had
choices.why: It was right three times in sixteen.

choices.text: A symptom alert like the burn rate
choices.why: The burn rate replaced it.

prompt: Paging only on the kept alerts would have meant 13 pages instead of 82. By what percentage would pages fall, to the nearest whole number?
Why is the verdict for a never-useful alert "remove or make it a ticket" rather than just "remove"?

choices.why: Tickets can be wrong too; they just cost no sleep.
Four alerts were removed or demoted.

choices.text: To keep the actionable rate high
choices.why: Tickets do not count as pages either way.

choices.text: Past pages say nothing of what is to come
choices.why: Right. The signal is kept where it costs no sleep.

prompt: What replaced the alert "card provider p99 over 2 s"?

choices.why: It was replaced by a page, not a ticket.
Right. It pages when shops wait long enough to count.
It stayed on the dashboard, and a symptom alert took its place.
Calling the provider is not an alert.

prompt: Which two cheap fixes does the lesson name for an alert that fires too eagerly?

choices.text: A louder ringtone and a second phone
choices.why: Neither changes when it fires.
That doubles the cost of each false page.

choices.text: A duration and a rate of change
choices.why: Right. Most real problems last longer than a minute.

choices.text: A lower threshold and more alerts
choices.why: That makes it fire more, not less.

prompt: Put the life of a new alert, under the Billing team's rule, in order.
items: written with its runbook and owner
runs as a ticket for two weeks

prompt: The lesson says deleting an alert feels dangerous and rarely is. Why rarely?

choices.text: A symptom alert would catch it anyway
choices.why: Right. Ask what would catch it instead.

choices.text: Because deleted alerts can be restored
choices.why: Restoring after the miss does not help.
Things break; the symptom alert sees them.
That is detection the team wants to avoid relying on.

prompt: Which item of the monthly review keeps a pruning from going too far?

choices.why: They show noise, not what was missed.
That item prunes; it does not check the pruning.
That adds alerts; it does not look for misses.
Right. A silent pager on a bad day is a failure too.

prompt: How can a team raise its actionable rate without changing a single alert?

choices.text: By adding more people to the rota
choices.why: The rate does not depend on headcount.
Right. On paper, every page needed a person.
Reviewing changes alerts.
The tool does not decide what counts as needed.

prompt: What does the Billing team report beside the actionable rate, and why?

choices.text: Raw counts, which are hard to dress up
choices.why: Right. Pages and night pages.

choices.text: Each person's response time, to rank them
choices.why: Nothing in the review ranks people.

choices.text: The error budget, to replace the rate
choices.why: The budget does not replace it.
The rate alone can be gamed.

prompt: What will the Billing team look at first after pruning, according to the lesson?

choices.text: Whether the count fell below ten
choices.why: The count comes second.
Lesson 17 handles that; this is about belief.

choices.text: Every page read within a minute
choices.why: Right. A page that people believe.
That is the budget's question.

prompt: An alert paged 16 times and 3 of those needed a person. What is its actionable rate, to the nearest whole percent?
Under the program's rule, an alert paged 10 times and 4 needed a person. What is the verdict?

choices.why: Keeping needs half or more.

choices.text: remove or make it a ticket
choices.why: That is for alerts that never needed anybody.
Not one of the verdicts.
Right. Between none and half.

prompt: The quarter had 25 night pages and the kept alerts account for 3. How many night pages would pruning have removed?
Which alert in the Billing team's list is a symptom?

choices.why: A cause; charges may be fine.
Right. A shop notices it.
A cause, filling over days.
A cause; the queue may drain.
